title: The Witness of Creation
english: He has very good reason, then, to call heaven and earth to witness. He was about to bring charges against Israel, and he wants the angels in heaven, and the whole earth itself, to know the ways of that people's impiety, so that no one would think that God had been moved without cause, or had rushed, over small and quite trivial faults, to cast off the beloved, the people set apart as His own portion, whom long ago He had rescued with very great strength from the greed of the Egyptians.

For He had mercy on them as a people wronged beyond all reason, weighed down by an unwilling servitude, contrary to the nobility that befitted their fathers and was native to them. And when their oppressors resisted, they were bitterly punished, as God hurled every kind of torment upon them. So, just as Israel's being taken up as His own was most conspicuous, He wants the manner of their casting off not to go unknown either.

If some would rather take it that the elements themselves are being called by the prophet's voice, the force of the thought would not miss the fitting sense, for those who have considered the following. Israel, as I said, was being redeemed through Moses from the ungodliness of the Egyptians. But when Pharaoh, impiously rising up against the commands of God, said, “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exodus 5:2), creation armed itself with its own Master against those who were hostile. From above, from heaven, came a great many striking signs, and likewise a great many wonders on the earth itself. Heaven sent down hail (Exodus 9:23), and the earth threw up frogs, as it is written (Exodus 8:6); the water was changed into blood (Exodus 7:20); and when furnace soot was scattered and clouded the air, sores and blisters broke out on the bodies of everyone (Exodus 9:8–10). So, since the very elements had all but laboured in vain over those who had been redeemed, he says: “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah 1:2).

But let us approach the sense of the passage in another way as well. Those of Israel dishonoured the training given through the Law and neglected the saving teachings; they forsook the one God, who is God by nature, and brought their worship to unclean demons on mountains and hills, and in the most thickly wooded ravines they burned incense to the works of their own hands and bowed down to them. The God of all was angered at this, and with very good reason, and He said to one of the holy prophets: “Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear, O hills, the judgment of the Lord, and you ravines, foundations of the earth, for the Lord has a judgment against His p…” (Micah 6:1–2).

title: The Shepherds' Folly and the Reproach of Jerusalem
english: …“My portion into a trackless wilderness. It has been made a ruin of destruction” (Jeremiah 12:10–11). And again: “For the shepherds have acted foolishly and have not sought the Lord; therefore the whole flock has not understood, and they have been scattered” (Jeremiah 10:21). The shepherds truly acted foolishly, and became a cause of ruin for the peoples under their hand.

And yet should they not rather, as men thoroughly instructed in the mystery of Christ through the Law and the Prophets, have become a road for the others toward believing in Him? But, as the Savior says, they received glory from man and did not seek the glory that comes from the only God (John 5:44). “For if they had believed Moses, they would have believed Him, for he wrote about Him” (John 5:46). So they have become blind, and guides of the blind (Matthew 15:14). In this way, too, they have slipped and fallen into the pits of destruction.

What then? The prophet tries to reshape them with good admonitions, so that they would choose to think better things and make trial of the Savior's words. For this purpose he usefully mixes rebuke into his admonitions, healing the wounds of their bad counsel with what is almost a remedy of many ingredients. That is why he says: “Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, you people of Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1:10). You hear how he brings down on peoples and rulers alike the rod that comes from love and from a godly mind, and strikes those gravely sick with disobedience.

He likens Jerusalem to the most impious cities, as one filled with a very great deal of sin and as having in herself no one at all [lacuna]. For the God of all was planning to burn the cities of the Sodomites, and He shared the matter with Abraham. Abraham said to Him: “Will You destroy the righteous with the ungodly? And shall the righteous be as the ungodly?” (Genesis 18:23). God promised that if ten righteous men were found in Sodom, He would hold back His wrath against them (Genesis 18:32). But they were not found. Therefore they paid penalties equal in measure to their own impieties. Such was Jerusalem, the slayer of the Lord, with her great scarcity of the righteous.

Indeed, the prophet Jeremiah pleaded earnestly for her, and God said: “Run through the streets of Jerusalem, and see, and know, and search in her squares, if you can find a man, if there is anyone who does justice and seeks faithfulness, and I will be merciful to her, says the Lord” (Jeremiah 5:1). Since, then, she is filthy, stained in many ways with the defilements of wickedness, and has a great scarcity of saints, he calls her Sodom and Gomorrah, and lays on peoples and leaders alike the reproach of the Sodomites' uncleanness. And what does he say? “Hear the word of the Lord, you rulers of Sodom; give heed to the law of God, you people of Go…” (Isaiah 1:10).

title: How the Faithful City Became a Harlot
english: “How has Zion, the faithful city full of justice, become a harlot? Righteousness once lodged in her, but now murderers” (Isaiah 1:21).

He is in a way astonished at the change in the synagogue of the Jews, so unsound and so without excuse: a change to the worse, I mean, and a passing from better things to more shameful ones. For by the Law given through Moses she was taught the knowledge of what is profitable, and since she had the word of God to guide her in each thing she was to do, she was splendid and highly esteemed and admirable, renowned for a great many men in whom the fruit of righteousness richly flowered, and she was worthy to be accepted by God. There were in her prophets and priests, and guardians of the works of righteousness, and leaders of the peoples who kept judgment, who had the Law on their tongue and were adorned with every good and excellent way of life.

Then she was bereft of all such men; or rather, she chose to take no account of that ancient goodness of hers and set at naught her reverence and love toward God. Before the coming of our Savior she bowed down to those who are not gods by nature, monstrously outraging the one and true Master by harlotries of this kind. Like some promiscuous and frenzied woman, she was impious in many ways, attaching herself now to some guides and now to others, men who knew how to lead her into anything at all that God hates. So the God of all accuses her through the voice of Jeremiah, saying: “See what the house of Israel has done to Me: she has gone up on every high mountain and under every leafy tree, and there she has played the harlot” (Jeremiah 3:6).

And again, as if to her: “If a man sends away his wife, and she goes from him and becomes another man's, will she ever return to him again? Will not that woman be utterly defiled? And you have played the harlot with many shepherds, and yet you kept returning to Me, says the Lord. Lift up your eyes and look straight ahead, and see where you have not been defiled. By the roads you sat for them like a lonely crow in the desert, and you have polluted the land with your harlotries and your wickedness, and you have had many shepherds as a stumbling block for yourself. You had the face of a harlot; you grew shameless toward all” (Jeremiah 3:1–3).

For, as I said, she despised service under God, turned to apostasy, and took unclean spirits and the worshippers of idols as her shepherds and teachers. These, as I said, were the charges against the synagogue of the Jews before the coming of our Savior. But when Christ shone upon those on earth — for, as it is written, “God is the Lord, and He has appeared to us” (Psalm 118:27) — she did not take Him as her teacher instead, but honoured teachings, commandments…
